lesson.title: Independent repetitions

steps.headline: For independent events, the chance that both happen is the two chances multiplied.

lead.text: A coin flip cannot change a die roll. Events like that are independent: learning one result leaves the other's chance as it was. Heads is 1/2 and a 3 is 1/6.
The chance of both is 1/2 × 1/6. You can check it on the grid of 12 results from the hook.
Roll two fair dice. The green square marks the pairs where both rolls are at most 3. Think about how big it looks next to the whole grid.

reveal.text: The square is 3 cells by 3, so 9 of 36. Each die is at most 3 with chance 1/2, and 1/2 × 1/2 agrees with your count.

steps.headline: Find the probability that two dice both show at most 4.

workedSteps.text: One die: four of the six values qualify.
The dice are independent, so multiply the chances.
Multiply the tops and the bottoms.

steps.headline: Find the probability that two dice both show at most 2.

workedSteps.text: One die: find the chance of at most 2.

lead.text: The same rule works for different kinds of event. Find each chance on its own, then multiply them.

reveal.text: You used the same rule on a coin and a die. Find each chance alone, then multiply.

steps.headline: Events that cannot happen together are not independent.

lead.text: Roll one die. “It shows 1” and “it shows 2” cannot both happen. Events like that are mutually exclusive. If you learn the die showed 1, you know it did not show 2.
Back to two dice. “At least one is above 3” is easy to count the other way round: it is everything except “both at most 3”.

reveal.text: You did not list the pairs. You took the complement of the both-low event, which independence let you find.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish independent events from mutually exclusive events, and calculate a joint probability.
lesson.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: You flip a coin and roll a die, and write down both results together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll multiply the chances of independent events, and tell independent events from ones that cannot both happen.

recap.keyIdea: When events are independent, the chance that both happen is the product of their chances. Events that cannot happen together are not independent.

blocks.text: You found that both dice at most 3 has chance 9/36, the same as 1/2 × 1/2. Then you multiplied again to get 1/9 for both at most 2.

recap.nextHook: Now from chance to data. What is a typical value in a list of numbers?

questions.prompt: Roll two fair dice. What is the probability that both show at most 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Count the 3 by 3 square among all 36 pairs.
Each individual roll passes for three of its six possible values.
Multiply three-sixths by three-sixths, then simplify the resulting fraction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each roll qualifies with probability 3/6 = 1/2; the joint probability is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: The 3 × 3 square is 9 of 36 cells, and 1/2 × 1/2 gives the same: independent chances multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one die alone. Both dice have to pass, so the chance is smaller than that.
Adding the two chances overshoots. Both must happen at once.

questions.prompt: Now what is the probability that both dice show at most 2? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Each individual probability is 2/6.
The matching cells form a two-by-two square.
Divide the area of that square by the six-by-six full outcome count.
questions.onCorrect: 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9. The four-cell square in the grid agrees.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one die. Both dice must pass.
That adds the two chances. Both must happen, so combine them another way.

questions.prompt: Why may you multiply the two chances?
hints: Independence concerns how a condition affects a probability.

acceptedIdeas: Knowing one event does not change the probability of the other
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Events are independent when learning that one occurred does not change the other's probability, when the conditional probability is defined. Equivalently, their joint probability is the product.

choices.label: Knowing one event does not change the probability of the other
Both events have probability one half

questions.onCorrect: Learning that one event happened leaves the other's chance unchanged. That is why the chances multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: Events that cannot happen together are mutually exclusive, which is different.
Independence is about whether one result changes the other's chance, not how large the chances are.

questions.prompt: What is the probability that at least one of the two dice shows above 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Subtract the chance that both rolls are low from 1.
Its complement is both rolls at most 3.
Subtract nine matching low-low pairs from the full grid and divide by the full count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both rolls at most 3 has probability 1/4. Subtracting this from 1 gives 3/4.

questions.onCorrect: 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. “At least one” is the complement of “both low”.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that both are low. The question asks about the pairs left over.
That is one die alone. Either die can be the high one.

questions.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed independently. What is the probability of two heads? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: List ordered coin outcomes.
Keep HT and TH separate when listing the possible pairs.
Divide the one heads-heads outcome by the full ordered outcome count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four equally likely ordered outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. Only HH qualifies: 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. It matches the one HH in four equally likely results.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one coin. Both coins have to show heads.
HH, HT, TH and TT are four results, not three. Keep HT and TH separate.

questions.prompt: On a single die roll, the events 'roll 1' and 'roll 2' are which kind of pair?
hints: Can both events occur in one roll?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The events are mutually exclusive: one roll cannot be both 1 and 2. They are not independent, because knowing that 1 occurred makes the probability of 2 zero.

questions.onCorrect: One roll can't show both 1 and 2, so they are mutually exclusive. Knowing one happened rules out the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Independent events can happen together. Here both cannot happen on one roll.
These are two separate events. Ask whether both can occur on one roll.

questions.prompt: You flip a coin and roll a die. One result is heads with a 3. How many different results are there?
hints: List the results that start with heads. How many are there?
Each coin result pairs with every die result.
Heads pairs with six die results. Tails does too.
questions.onCorrect: 12: every coin result pairs with every die result. Keep that grid in mind.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sides: 2 + 6. Each coin result pairs with every die result, so think of a grid.
That is only the heads results. Tails pairs with the die results as well.

questions.prompt: One fair die is rolled. What is the probability that it shows at most 2? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Which values are at most 2?
Two of the six values qualify.
Put the number of qualifying values over the number of values.
questions.onCorrect: 1/3. Two of the six equally likely values qualify.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts values. A probability divides by the six possible values.
Count 1 and 2 both; two values qualify.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of tails and a number above 4? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: Find each chance alone: tails, then a number above 4.
Tails is one of two results. Which die numbers are above 4?
The two chances are independent, so combine them with the rule from the worked example.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tails is 1/2. A 5 or 6 is 2/6 = 1/3. Together: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.

questions.onCorrect: 1/6. The coin and die are independent, so multiply 1/2 by 1/3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of not getting both. Multiply the two separate chances.
Adding the chances is for exclusive events. Here both must happen: multiply them.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped three times. What is the probability of three heads? Give a fraction or a decimal to three places.
hints: One flip shows heads with probability 1/2. Does the first flip change the second?
The flips are independent. How many chances do you multiply?
Multiply the chance for each flip together.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each flip is 1/2 and the flips are independent: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

questions.onCorrect: 1/8. Independent flips multiply: each extra heads halves the chance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one flip. All three have to be heads, which makes the chance smaller.
That is two flips. There is a third to include.
Adding the chances gives more than 1, which can't be a probability. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of tails and an even number? Give a fraction or a decimal.
hints: Find the chance of tails alone, then of an even number alone.
Even numbers on a die are 2, 4 and 6. What fraction is that?
The two are independent, so combine the two chances as the lesson says.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one of the two chances. Both must happen.
Adding the chances overshoots. Both must happen at once.

questions.prompt: One die is rolled. Are “shows 1” and “shows an even number” mutually exclusive?
hints: Is the number 1 odd or even?

acceptedIdeas: Yes: one roll cannot be both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1 is odd, so a roll cannot show 1 and an even number together.

choices.label: Yes: one roll cannot be both
No: both can happen on one roll

questions.onCorrect: Yes. One roll cannot be both, so they are mutually exclusive.

misconceptions.feedback: The first number is odd. Ask whether a roll can be odd and even at once.

citations.claim: Independent events do not change each other's chances, so the joint probability is the product.
Both rolls at most 3 is a 3 by 3 square of 36 cells, which equals 1/2 × 1/2.
For independent dice both at most 4 has probability 2/3 × 2/3 = 4/9.
Each die is at most 2 with chance 1/3, so both is 1/9.
A coin and a die are independent, so their chances multiply.
Mutually exclusive events cannot both occur, so learning one changes the other's chance.
At least one high is the complement of both low.
A coin result pairs with each die result, giving 2 × 6 = 12 results.
Both at most 3 has probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Both at most 2 has 2 × 2 = 4 pairs, so 4/36 = 1/9.
Events are independent when learning one does not change the other's probability; then the joint probability is the product.
Both low has probability 1/4; subtracting from 1 gives 3/4.
Two fair coins: HH is one of four equally likely outcomes, 1/4.
One roll cannot be both 1 and 2, so the events are mutually exclusive, not independent.
Two of six die values are at most 2: 1/3.
Tails is 1/2 and above 4 is 1/3; independent, so 1/6.
Three independent flips: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.
Each roll has probability 1/6, so both have probability 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together; that is different from independence.
For independent events the chance of both is the product of their chances.
Events that cannot both occur on one trial are mutually exclusive.
